name: Antony the Great
knownFor: The Egyptian hermit whose withdrawal to the desert, and the Life written of him, drew monks after him and spread monasticism east and west.
dates: Born 251, died 356, in Ernest Cushing Richardson's note to Jerome; the Life gives his age at death as "near a hundred and five"
place: Coma, near Heraclea in Egypt (Sozomen), and the Egyptian desert
role: Hermit and father of the desert monks

keyWorks.title: Seven Letters
keyWorks.about: letters in Coptic to various monasteries, which Jerome of Strido says were translated into Greek; none is held in this Library

traces: Monks who settled the Egyptian desert in his lifetime, so that the Life says "the desert was colonised by monks."

A pattern of withdrawal that spread west. In his Confessions, Augustine of Hippo tells how two court officials read the Life and resolved to leave the court and serve God, and how hearing of Antony moved him.
remembered: The Life of Antony, long read as the work of Athanasius of Alexandria, carried his name across the Latin West.
Jerome of Strido modeled his own Life of Hilarion on it, and Robertson notes it "kindled the flame of monastic aspirations" at Rome and across the West.

uncertain: Antony's life is known chiefly from the Life of Antony, a work of praise. Archibald Robertson, its editor, grants there is "idealisation, panegyric" in it.

The Life's writer says he was Antony's attendant and "poured water on his hands." Robertson notes that some manuscripts, Greek and Latin, make the attendant someone else, and that the text "requires further sifting."

Who wrote the Life is disputed. The church has long given it to Athanasius of Alexandria. Robertson holds the dispute open but judges "the external evidence for the Vita is too strong to allow us to set it aside as spurious." He also records that Gwatkin went so far as to pronounce that Antony "never existed," and calls that far ahead of the evidence.
Jerome says Antony's seven Coptic letters were translated into Greek. None is held in this Library, so Antony's own voice cannot be checked here against the Life.

quotationOriginals.modern: the desert became a city of monks.
quotationOriginals.printed: καὶ ἡ ἔρημος ἐπολίσθη ὑπὸ μοναχῶν
quotationOriginals.work: Life of Antony §14, Greek, Migne, PG 26
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The OCR prints a note marker "(38)" inside the phrase. The 1892 English (npnf204, line 31625) reads "the desert was colonised by monks"; "colonised" now suggests conquest.

quotationOriginals.modern: For I had heard this of Antony. He had come in by chance during the Gospel reading, and was urged on by it. It was as though the words read were spoken to him.
quotationOriginals.printed: audieram enim de Antonio, quod ex euangelica lectione, cui forte superuenerat, admonitus fuerit, tamquam sibi diceretur quod legebatur
quotationOriginals.uncertain: "Urged on" renders admonitus, which means warned or prompted. The Pilkington English (npnf101, lines 13117-13121) reads "he received the admonition as if what was read were addressed to him".

briefReferences: Life of Antony §1–2: his Christian parents of good family and wealth; their death when he was about eighteen or twenty; the Gospel reading, the fields given to the villagers, the rest sold for the poor.
Life §3–4, §7: the hermits near the villages, the old man of the next village, work with his hands, bread and salt once a day.
Life, prologue, and Robertson's introduction: the authorship long credited to Athanasius, and the date, 356–362.
Life §12, §14: the deserted fort across the river, the walled door, bread twice a year; the door forced after nearly twenty years; "the desert became a city of monks" (Greek, PG 26).
Life §49–50: crowds and healings; three days into the desert to the mountain with a spring.
Life §69: against the Arians in Alexandria; the Son of God not created.
Life §89–91: near a hundred and five; burial in secret, against the Egyptian custom of keeping the holy dead in houses.
Life, prologue and §93: a pattern for monks abroad; heard of in Spain, Gaul, Rome and Africa.
Robertson's introduction: the Latin translation by Evagrius of Antioch.
Life §81: Constantine and his sons wrote to him.
Augustine, Confessions VIII.6.14–15: Pontitianus, the two officials at Trier. VIII.12.29: the garden at Milan, Antony and the Gospel reading, the letters of Paul.
